title: Small models — what we cut, and what should be left in its place
intro: A small model cannot hold everything the assistant would normally be given, so something has to go. Today three different kinds of file are handled three different ways, and only one of those ways was ever decided on purpose — the others are how the code happened to grow. Your project rules are OUTLINED: every heading survives at any size, and the assistant is told which file to read for the detail. A skill is CUT at a character count, mid-sentence, and told nothing about where it came from. Add-on tool sets are DROPPED whole, from the end of your list, until the rest fits. For comparison: opencode hands the assistant a skill's folder and file paths so it can go and read more, but injects your rules file whole with no limit at all — one 331KB rules file used 81 percent of a large window before any work started, and their request for a size limit was closed without action. Hermes cuts a file 70 percent from the front and 20 percent from the end, keeping both ends with a marker in the middle, and refuses to run at all below a 64k window. Cline, Roo and Goose do not manage instruction size at all — they summarise the conversation instead. None of them tell you what was cut. These seven questions decide what we do.

steps.surface: Any chat on a small model
steps.path: Not a screen — this is what the assistant is handed when a chat starts
steps.headline: When a file is too big to fit, what should the assistant get instead of the whole thing?
steps.today: It depends which file, and not on purpose. Your project rules are outlined — every heading survives and it is told which file to read for the rest. A skill is cut at a character count, wherever that lands, and told nothing.
steps.problem: A cut-off procedure is worse than no procedure. The assistant follows the half it received believing that is the whole thing. Step 7 of 9 simply does not exist, and nothing anywhere says so.
steps.proposal: Pick one shape for a cut and use it for everything.

options.label: Outline it, and name the file
pros: Every heading survives, so the assistant always knows the full shape of what it was given.
It knows which file to read when it needs one step in full.
Already built and already trusted — it is exactly what your project rules use today.
cons: The detail under most headings is missing until it goes and reads it.
Reading the file costs a turn, so the first step is slower.

options.label: Keep both ends, mark the middle
options.summary: What Hermes does: 70 percent from the front, 20 percent from the end.
pros: Keeps the ending, where procedures usually put the finishing steps — a front-only cut always loses those.
Simple, and the same every time.
cons: The middle disappears with no heading left behind, so the assistant cannot tell what it is missing.
Still hands over a fragment; just a differently shaped one.

options.label: Leave it out entirely and say so
pros: No half-followed procedure — the assistant knows it does not have the thing.
The clearest possible signal that something is missing.
cons: Throws away material that would have fitted.
A skill you asked for by name does nothing at all.

steps.surface: Any chat on a small model
steps.path: What happens after the assistant is told to go and read the rest
steps.headline: If the assistant is told to go read a file, should that cost you a permission prompt?
steps.today: Skills you install live outside your project folder, and the assistant's file reading is fenced to the project. So following a pointer to a skill would raise the "this is outside your project — allow?" prompt.
steps.problem: We would be handing the assistant an instruction it cannot follow without interrupting you — and interrupting you to approve reading a file the app itself chose to give it a moment earlier.
steps.proposal: Treat a file the app injected as already approved for the assistant to re-read.

options.label: Free to re-read what the app gave it
pros: A pointer actually works, instead of stopping to ask you.
You are never asked to approve something the app already decided to include.
Narrow by design — only files the app itself injected, not a general loosening of the fence.
cons: One more path that reads outside your project folder, even if a narrow one.
The fence becomes a rule with an exception, which is harder to explain.

options.label: Keep the fence, approve each time
pros: Nothing outside your project is ever read without you saying so.
No new code path and nothing new to explain.
cons: Every cut skill costs you an approval prompt in the middle of a task.
Most people will approve without reading it, which teaches exactly the wrong habit.

steps.intro: Skills are the worst-served thing we have. There are two ways into one and they behave completely differently — not by decision, but because they were written at different times.

steps.path: Typing a skill's name, versus the assistant choosing one itself
steps.headline: The two ways into a skill behave differently. Should they be made the same?
steps.today: When the assistant picks a skill itself it gets the whole file, limited only by a flat 30,000-character ceiling no matter how small the model is. When you type the skill's name, it is cut to fit the model. On a small model only the second way exists at all.
steps.problem: The same skill arrives in two different sizes depending on who asked for it. And the flat ceiling can hand a small model roughly half its entire working memory in one go.
steps.proposal: Put both routes through the same fitting.

options.label: Same fitting both ways
pros: A skill is the same skill however it was reached.
Stops a single skill from swallowing a small model's whole working memory.
One behaviour to explain in the panel instead of two.
cons: On mid-size models, the route where the assistant chooses gets less text than it does today.

options.label: Leave them as they are
pros: No change, and the assistant-chosen route keeps as much detail as it can.
cons: The mismatch stays, and the flat ceiling goes on being the wrong size for small models.
The panel has to describe two behaviours for one thing.

steps.path: Typing a skill's name on a model too small to hold it
steps.headline: You asked for a skill by name and it does not fit. Half of it, or none of it?
steps.today: You get as much as fits, cut mid-sentence, with a note saying it was shortened.
steps.problem: You asked for that skill deliberately, so you want it to run. But a procedure cut in half can be followed wrongly with complete confidence, which is worse than being told plainly that it will not fit.
steps.proposal: Decide what happens when you explicitly ask for something too big.

options.label: Outline it and start anyway
pros: It runs, and every step is at least named.
It can read the detail of a step at the moment it reaches that step.
cons: Slower, because it stops to read.
On a very small model even the headings may crowd out the work.

options.label: Refuse, and tell you why
pros: No half-run procedure, ever.
You can switch to a bigger model before wasting a turn.
cons: A skill you asked for does nothing at all.
Frustrating when the skill would have mostly worked.

options.label: As much as fits, as today
pros: It always does something, and sometimes the first half is all you needed.
cons: The most likely route to confidently wrong work.
The assistant cannot tell you which steps it never saw.

steps.intro: Three decisions about how far we go to support models that are genuinely too small, and what we owe you when we cannot fit everything.

steps.surface: Any chat on a small model
steps.path: What gets left out when there is not room for everything
steps.headline: When there is not room for everything, what should be given up first?
steps.today: Add-on tool sets go first — whole ones are dropped from the end of your list until the rest fits. Then rules and skills are shrunk to what is left. Nothing asks you, and nothing has ever decided this order.
steps.problem: The order is a consequence of how the code grew. For some projects the add-on tools are the entire point of the setup; for others the written rules are.
steps.proposal: Confirm the order, or let it be set per project.

options.label: Keep today's order, but show it
pros: Tool descriptions cost tokens on every single turn, so dropping them frees the most room for the least loss.
The panel being built will show exactly which ones went and why.
Nothing new for you to configure.
cons: An add-on you depend on can disappear in the project where it mattered most.

options.label: Let each project set the order
pros: A project that lives on one add-on can protect it.
Puts the choice with the person who knows what matters.
cons: A setting most people will never find, for a problem they did not know they had.
Another thing to maintain and explain.

options.label: Rules first, then skills, then tools
pros: Your written instructions are never touched, whatever the model.
cons: Tools are what the assistant acts with — keeping every rule and losing the tools leaves it well-informed and unable to do anything.
Rules are the cheapest thing to shorten well, since outlining already works.

steps.path: Starting a chat on a very small local model
steps.headline: Hermes and opencode refuse to run below 64k. Should we have a floor too?
steps.today: We run on anything and quietly do less. Below 32k the assistant stops choosing skills for itself, and everything it is given is squeezed into a small allowance.
steps.problem: Supporting genuinely small models is a real difference for us — the others simply refuse. But a model that is too small does bad work, and people blame the app, not the model.
steps.proposal: Decide where the honest line sits between refusing outright and quietly doing less.

options.label: Run anything, say plainly what is reduced
pros: Keeps the thing that makes us different from every other tool.
The panel already tells them what was cut and why, which none of the others do.
Their hardware and their choice, made with the facts in front of them.
cons: Someone can still have a poor first experience on a model that was never going to work.
Explaining a reduced experience is harder than refusing one.

options.label: Warn before the first message, then continue
pros: The warning arrives before the work rather than after it.
Still their choice.
cons: One more thing to click past, and people click past warnings.
Hard to word without sounding like the app itself is broken.

options.label: Refuse below a floor, as the others do
pros: Nobody gets a bad experience from a hopeless model.
Simplest thing to support and explain.
cons: Throws away our clearest difference from everyone else.
A 16k model is genuinely useful for short single-file work, and this would ban it.

steps.path: Changing the model halfway through a conversation
steps.headline: Switching to a smaller model mid-chat does not re-fit anything. Fix it, or say so?
steps.today: What the assistant is given is worked out once, when the chat starts. Change the model halfway through and none of it is redone.
steps.problem: Switch from a big model to a small one and it is handed more than it can hold — Hermes has this exact bug open right now. Switch the other way and you keep a small model's cuts for no reason.
steps.proposal: Either redo the fitting when the model changes, or say plainly that the figures are from when the chat started.

options.label: Say plainly it is from the start of the chat
pros: Honest, and costs nothing to build.
Redoing it mid-chat rewrites what was already sent, which makes every later turn slower and more expensive on a local model.
The panel can simply date the figures.
cons: The mismatch is still real — you just know about it.
A long chat after a model switch may quietly behave worse than the panel suggests.

options.label: Redo the fitting on every switch
pros: What the assistant holds always matches the model actually answering.
Removes a whole class of confusing behaviour.
cons: Rewrites the beginning of the conversation, so a local model must re-read the whole chat — noticeably slower and more expensive from then on.
More moving parts in the one piece of code that must never break.

options.label: Ask you to start a fresh chat instead
pros: Always correct, and simple to build and explain.
cons: You lose the conversation you were in the middle of.
Switching models mid-task is one of the most useful things about the app.
